lesson.title: When Sigma Is a Mystery: Meet the T-Distribution
lesson.summary: The t-distribution is the sampling distribution used when the population standard deviation is unknown and estimated from the sample, and it has heavier tails than the normal distribution to account for that extra uncertainty.
lesson.body:
Every z-procedure you have used so far, for a proportion, or for a mean with a known population standard deviation, relies on knowing sigma exactly. In practice, though, the population standard deviation is almost never known. What you actually have is s, the sample standard deviation, calculated from the same data used to calculate the sample mean. Substituting s for sigma seems like a small change, but it has a real consequence: s is itself a statistic, computed from a random sample, so it varies from sample to sample. That extra layer of randomness makes the resulting standardized statistic, t = (xbar - mu) / (s / square root of n), more variable than a standardized statistic that uses the true, fixed sigma. The probability distribution that correctly accounts for this extra variability is called the t-distribution.

The t-distribution is, like the normal distribution, symmetric and bell-shaped and centered at 0. But it is not identical to the standard normal curve: it has heavier tails, meaning more probability sits out in the extreme values, and a slightly shorter, wider peak. This makes sense given where the extra uncertainty comes from. Because s can, by chance, come out smaller than the true sigma in a given sample, the standardized statistic t can swing to more extreme values more often than a z-statistic would, and the distribution has to spread that extra probability into its tails to stay accurate.

The t-distribution is not a single curve but a whole family of curves, one for each possible value of degrees of freedom, and for a one-sample situation that degrees of freedom is n - 1, exactly the quantity from the previous section. With very few degrees of freedom, meaning a very small sample, s is a poor, highly variable estimate of sigma, so the t-distribution for a small df has notably heavier tails than the normal curve. As degrees of freedom grows, meaning larger samples, s becomes a more precise, stable estimate of sigma, the extra uncertainty shrinks, and the t-distribution's tails grow thinner and thinner, hugging the standard normal curve more and more closely. In the limit, as degrees of freedom approaches infinity, the t-distribution becomes indistinguishable from the standard normal distribution. This relationship, between the t-distribution and the normal curve it converges to, is explored directly in the next section.
